title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How Sir Pellias Fought Sir Engamore, Also Called the Knight of the Green Sleeves, and What Happened to the Lady Ettard._

Sir Pellias and his party, together with the damsel Parcenet and hers, traveled onward until, late in the afternoon, they came to the far edge of the forest. There the woods ended altogether. Before them, under the open sky, lay many fields and meadows, with farms, small cottages, and groves of trees all in bloom with tender leaves and sweet-smelling blossoms.

Sir Pellias said, “This is truly a beautiful land that we have come into.” The damsel Parcenet was very pleased, and she said, “Sir, I am glad that what you see pleases you. All this region belongs to the Lady Ettard, and it is my home. Besides, from the top of that hill over there you can see the castle of Grantmesnle, which lies in the valley below.” Then Sir Pellias said, “Let us hurry! I am eager to see that place.”

So they spurred their horses and rode up the hill at a steady gallop. When they reached the top, they saw the Castle of Grantmesnle lying below them, as small and clear as if it rested on the palm of a hand. Sir Pellias saw that it was a very fair castle. Its outer walls were built of red stone, and inside the walls stood many buildings of red brick. Behind the walls lay a little town, and from where they stood they could see its streets and the people coming and going about their business. Sir Pellias admired the castle and said, “Truly, maiden, that is a fine estate.”
“Yes,” said Parcenet, “those of us who live there think it a very fine estate indeed.”

Then Sir Pellias said to Parcenet, “Maiden, that glade of young trees near the castle looks like a cheerful spot. We will make our camp there, my companions in arms and I. We will also have three pavilions set up to shelter us by day and by night. In the meantime, I ask you to go to the lady, your mistress, and tell her that a knight has come here who does not know her, but who holds that the Lady Guinevere of Camelot is the fairest lady in all the world. Tell her also that I am here to defend those words against all comers, at the risk of my own life. So if the lady has any champion to fight for her, I will meet him in that field tomorrow at midday, a little before I eat my noon meal. At that time I mean to ride into the field and parade there until my friends call me in to dinner. I will take my stand in that place in honor of the Lady Guinevere of Camelot.”

“Sir Pellias,” said the damsel, “I will do just as you ask. I cannot wish for you to win that fight, and yet I am truly sorry to leave you. You are both a very brave and a very gentle knight, and I find that I have grown fond of you.”
Then Sir Pellias laughed and said, “Parcenet, you give me more praise than I deserve.” And Parcenet said, “Sir, that is not so. You deserve everything good I can say about you.”

Then the two of them parted with good will and much kindness. The maiden and the three pages went one way. Sir Pellias, his two companions, and the several attendants they had brought went into the glade of young trees, just as Sir Pellias had ordered.

There they set up three pavilions in the shade of the trees. The first was of fair white cloth, the second of green cloth, and the third of scarlet cloth. Over each pavilion they set a banner showing the device of the knight it belonged to. Above the white pavilion was the device of Sir Pellias, which was three swans on a silver field. Above the red pavilion, which belonged to Sir Brandiles, was a red banner showing his device, a mailed hand gripping a hammer. Above the green pavilion, which belonged to Sir Mador de la Porte, was a green banner with his device, a carrion crow holding a white lily in one claw and a sword in the other.

The next day, when midday was near, Sir Pellias rode out into the field before the castle, as he had promised. He was dressed from head to foot in the red armor he had taken from the body of Sir Adresack, and in that armor he looked terrifying. He rode up and down before the castle walls for a good while, crying in a loud voice, “Hear me! Hear me! Here stands a knight of King Arthur’s Court and of his Round Table. He declares, and is ready to defend with his own body, that the Lady Guinevere, King Arthur’s Queen of Camelot, is the most beautiful lady in all the world, without exception. So if any knight says otherwise, let him come out at once and defend his opinion.”

After Sir Pellias appeared in the meadow, a great stir rose inside the castle. Many people climbed onto the walls and looked down at Sir Pellias as he rode about the field. After a time the drawbridge of the castle was lowered, and a knight rode out, very large of body and very proud in manner. He was dressed from head to foot in green armor, and he wore a green sleeve on each arm. For this reason he was sometimes called the Knight of the Green Sleeves.

The Green Knight rode toward Sir Pellias, and Sir Pellias rode toward the Green Knight. When they met, they greeted each other with great politeness and knightly courtesy. Then the Green Knight said to Sir Pellias, “Sir Knight, will you do me the great favor of telling me your name?”
Sir Pellias answered, “Gladly. I am Sir Pellias, a knight of King Arthur’s Court and of his Round Table.”

Then the Green Knight replied, “Ha, Sir Pellias, it is a great honor to face so famous a knight. Who in the Courts of Chivalry has not heard of you? If I am lucky enough to overthrow you, all your honor will become mine. In return for your courtesy in telling me your name, I will give you mine and my title. I am Sir Engamore of Malverat, also known as the Knight of the Green Sleeves. I will also tell you that I am the champion of the Lady Ettard of Grantmesnle. For eleven months I have defended her claim to be the most beautiful lady alive, against all comers. If I defend it successfully for one month more, I will win her hand and all this fair estate. So I am ready to do everything in my power in her honor.”
Then Sir Pellias said, “Sir Knight, I thank you for your greeting, and I too will do all I can in this fight.” Then each knight saluted the other with his lance, and each rode to his appointed place.

A great crowd of people had come down to the lower walls of the castle and the town to watch the contest that was about to begin. It would be hard to imagine a finer occasion for knights to meet in a glorious joust. Each knight made himself ready in every way and set his spear and lance with great care. When all was ready, a herald who had come out from the castle into the field gave the signal to charge. In an instant each knight drove his spurs into his horse and rushed at the other with such terrible speed that the ground shook and trembled under the beating of the horses’ feet. They met exactly in the center of the field, each striking the other in the middle of his defenses with a force that was terrible to see. The spear of Sir Engamore burst into as many as thirty pieces. But the spear of Sir Pellias held firm, and the Green Knight was hurled out of his saddle so violently that he struck the ground more than a spear’s length behind his horse’s tail.

When the people on the walls saw how completely the Green Knight had been overthrown, they raised a great outcry, for there was no other knight in all those parts like Sir Engamore. The Lady Ettard cried out loudest of all, for she loved Sir Engamore dearly. Seeing him flung so violently to the ground, she thought he might have been killed.

Three squires ran to Sir Engamore, lifted him up, and unlaced his helmet to give him air. They saw that he was not dead, but only in a deep faint. After a while he opened his eyes, and Sir Pellias was very glad, for it would have grieved him to have killed that knight. When Sir Engamore came to his senses again, he demanded fiercely that he be allowed to continue the contest with Sir Pellias on foot, with swords. But Sir Pellias would not agree. “No, Sir Engamore,” he said, “I will not fight you over so serious a quarrel as that, for I have no ill will against you.” At this refusal Sir Engamore began to weep, out of sheer anger and shame at being so completely overthrown.

Then Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte came and praised Sir Pellias highly for the fine way he had fought in the contest. At the same time they spoke kindly to Sir Engamore and comforted him for his misfortune. But Sir Engamore took little comfort from their words.

While they were all standing together, the Lady Ettard came out from the castle with a very cheerful and handsome company of squires and ladies. They crossed the meadow toward the place where Sir Pellias and the others stood.
When Sir Pellias saw the lady approaching, he drew his dagger, cut the straps of his helmet, and took the helmet off his head. Then he went forward bareheaded to meet her.

But when he came close to her, he saw that she was many times more beautiful than the picture of her painted on the ivory panel that he had seen before. His heart went out to her with a very strong liking. So he knelt down on the grass and pressed his hands together, palm to palm, before her. He said, “Lady, I beg your forgiveness for having fought against your claim. I did it only for my Queen. Otherwise I would rather have been your champion than the champion of any other lady I have ever seen.”

At that time Sir Pellias wore around his neck the collar of emeralds, opals, and gold that the Lady of the Lake had given him. When the Lady Ettard looked at him, that necklace drew her heart toward him with a powerful enchantment. She smiled warmly at Sir Pellias, gave him her hand, and helped him rise from where he knelt. And she said to him, “Sir Knight, you are a very famous warrior. I think there is no one who knows anything of chivalry who has not heard of the fame of Sir Pellias, the Gentle Knight. My champion Sir Engamore of Malverat has overthrown every challenger until now, but he need not feel very ashamed to have been overthrown by so terribly strong a knight.”

Sir Pellias was very glad of the kind words the Lady Ettard spoke to him, and he introduced her to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. The Lady Ettard spoke very graciously to these knights too, moved by the great regard she felt for Sir Pellias. She invited them to come into the castle and refresh themselves with good cheer, and the knights said they would soon do so. They returned, each to his own pavilion, and there each dressed himself in fine clothing and ornaments of gold and silver, until he made noble company for any Court. Then the three knights went to the castle of Grantmesnle, and when they arrived, everyone was amazed at their noble appearance.
But Sir Engamore, who had by now recovered from his fall, was deeply discouraged. He said to himself, “Who am I, beside these noble lords?” So he stood apart, heavy-hearted and low in spirit.

Then the Lady Ettard held a very fine feast, and Sir Pellias, Sir Brandiles, and Sir Mador de la Porte were delighted with it. She seated Sir Pellias at her right hand and Sir Engamore at her left. This made Sir Engamore feel still worse, for until now he had always sat at the right hand of the Lady Ettard.

Because Sir Pellias wore the wonderful collar that the Lady of the Lake had given him, the Lady Ettard could not take her eyes from him. After they had refreshed themselves and gone out to walk in the warm sunshine of the castle gardens, she wanted Sir Pellias beside her constantly. When it came time for the visiting knights to leave the castle, she begged Sir Pellias to stay a while longer. Sir Pellias was very glad to do so, for he was delighted beyond measure by the kindness and the beauty of the Lady Ettard.
So after a while Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte went back to their pavilions, and Sir Pellias stayed on in the castle of Grantmesnle a little longer.

That night the Lady Ettard had a supper prepared for herself and Sir Pellias. She and Sir Pellias sat alone at the table, and the damsel Parcenet waited on the lady. While they ate, some young pages and squires played sweetly on harps, and some maidens of the lady’s Court sang so sweetly that it lifted the heart of anyone who heard them. Sir Pellias was so enchanted by the sweet music and by the beauty of the Lady Ettard that he did not know whether he was on earth or in Paradise. In his great happiness he said to the Lady Ettard, “Lady, I wish I could do something for you, to show you how high my regard and honor for you is.”

As Sir Pellias sat beside her, the Lady Ettard had kept her eyes on the wonderful collar of gold, emeralds, and opals that hung around his neck, and she wanted it very badly. So she now said to Sir Pellias, “Sir Knight, you could do me a great favor, if you are willing.” “What favor can I do you, Lady?” said Sir Pellias. “Sir,” said the Lady Ettard, “you can give me that collar that hangs around your neck.”
At this the face of Sir Pellias fell, and he said, “Lady, I cannot do that. That collar came to me in such an extraordinary way that I cannot part with it.”
Then the Lady Ettard said, “Why can you not part with it, Sir Pellias?”
Then Sir Pellias told her the whole of that extraordinary adventure with the Lady of the Lake, and how that fairy lady had given him the collar.

The Lady Ettard was greatly astonished at this, and she said, “Sir Pellias, that is a very wonderful story. Even so, though you cannot give that collar to me, you could let me wear it for a little while. I am charmed beyond all measure by the beauty of that collar, so I beg you to let me wear it for a little.”
At last Sir Pellias could not say no to her any longer. “Lady, you may wear it for a while,” he said. Then he lifted the collar from around his neck and hung it around the neck of the Lady Ettard.

After a short time the power of the jewel left Sir Pellias and passed into the Lady Ettard. She now looked at Sir Pellias with very different eyes than before. She said to herself, “Ha! What was wrong with me, that I let that knight enchant me, when my own champion has served me so faithfully? Has this knight not done me terrible wrong? Did he not come here for that very purpose? Did he not defeat my own true knight to show his scorn for me? Why did I ever treat him with such favor as I have?” Yet though she thought all this, she gave Sir Pellias no sign of it. She seemed to laugh and talk cheerfully. All the same, she began at once to search her mind for a way to take revenge on him. She said to herself, “Look! Is he not my enemy, and is my enemy not now in my power? Why should I not take full revenge on him for everything he has done to us of Grantmesnle?”

Soon she made an excuse, rose, and left Sir Pellias. She drew the damsel Parcenet aside and said, “Go and bring me a strong sleeping-draught right away.” Parcenet asked, “Lady, what do you mean to do?” The Lady Ettard answered, “Never mind.” Parcenet said, “Would you give that noble knight a sleeping-draught?” The lady said, “I would.” Then Parcenet said, “Lady, that would surely be a wicked thing to do to a man who sits peacefully at your table and eats your bread and salt.” The Lady Ettard replied, “Do not worry about that, girl. Just go at once and do as I tell you.”

Parcenet saw that it was not wise to disobey the lady, so she went at once and did as she was told. She brought the sleeping-draught to the lady in a cup of pure wine. The Lady Ettard took the cup and said to Sir Pellias, “Take this cup of wine, Sir Knight, and drink it to me, as much as you wish me well.” Parcenet stood behind her lady’s chair, and when Sir Pellias took the cup, she frowned and shook her head at him. But Sir Pellias did not see her. He was dizzy with the beauty of the Lady Ettard and with the enchantment of the collar of emeralds, opal stones, and gold that she now wore. So he said to her, “Lady, if there were poison in this cup, I would still drink the wine at your command.”
At that the Lady Ettard burst out laughing and said, “Sir Knight, there is no poison in that cup.”
Sir Pellias took the cup and drank the wine. Then he said, “Lady, what is this? The wine tastes bitter.” The Lady Ettard answered, “Sir, that cannot be.”

Soon Sir Pellias felt his head grow terribly heavy, as if it were made of lead, and he lowered it onto the table where he sat. The Lady Ettard kept watching him with a strange look. After a while she said, “Sir Knight, are you asleep?” Sir Pellias did not answer, for the fumes of the sleeping-draught had risen into his brain, and he was asleep.

Then the Lady Ettard rose laughing, clapped her hands together, and called her attendants. She said to them, “Take this knight away and carry him into an inner room. When you have brought him there, strip off his fine clothes and his ornaments, so that he has nothing left on but his underclothes. Then lay him on a pallet and carry him out of the castle, into the meadow below the walls where he defeated Sir Engamore. In the morning he will be a mockery and a joke to everyone who sees him. So we will shame him in the same field where he defeated Sir Engamore, and his shame will be greater than Sir Engamore’s.”
When the damsel Parcenet heard this, she was deeply grieved. She went off by herself and wept for Sir Pellias. But the others took Sir Pellias and did to him just as the Lady Ettard had ordered.

When morning came, Sir Pellias woke with the sun shining in his face. He did not know where he was at all, for his mind was clouded by the sleeping-draught he had drunk. He said to himself, “Am I dreaming, or am I awake? Truly, the last thing I remember is sitting at supper with the Lady Ettard, and yet here I am in an open field with the sun shining on me.”

He raised himself on his elbow, and he saw that he was lying beneath the castle walls, near the small back gate. Above him, on top of the wall, a great crowd of people had gathered. When they saw that he was awake, they laughed and jeered at him. The Lady Ettard also looked down at him from a window, and he saw that she was laughing at him and enjoying herself. Then he saw that he lay there dressed only in his linen undershirt and with bare feet, as if he were ready to sleep for the night. He sat up on the cot and said to himself, “Surely this must be some shameful dream that weighs on me.” He could not shake off his bewilderment.

As he sat there, the back gate suddenly opened, and the damsel Parcenet came out. Her face was wet with tears, and she carried a flame-colored cloak in her hand. She ran straight to Sir Pellias and said, “You good and gentle knight, take this and wrap yourself in it.”

Then Sir Pellias knew that this was no dream but a true and terrible disgrace. He was seized by such deep shame that he began to shake, and his teeth chattered as if he had a fever. He said to Parcenet, “Maiden, I thank you.” He could find no more words to say. He took the cloak and wrapped himself in it.

When the people on the walls saw what Parcenet had done, they booed her and shouted many cruel words at her. The maiden ran back into the castle. Sir Pellias got up and made his way toward his pavilion, wrapped in the cloak. As he went, he staggered and stumbled like a drunken man, for he carried a burden of shame that was almost too heavy to bear.

When Sir Pellias reached his pavilion, he went in, threw himself face down on his couch, and lay there without a word. Soon Sir Brandiles and Mador de la Porte heard of the trouble that had come upon Sir Pellias. They hurried to where he lay and grieved greatly over him. They were also very angry at the shame that had been put on him. They said, “We will get help from Camelot, break into that castle, and bring the Lady Ettard here to beg your pardon for this insult. We will do this even if we have to drag her here by the hair of her head.”

But Sir Pellias did not lift his head. He only groaned and said, “Leave it, good sirs. You must not do that, under any circumstances, because she is a woman. Even now I would defend her honor, even if I died doing it. I do not know whether I am bewitched or what is wrong with me, but I love her with a great passion, and I cannot tear my heart away from her.”
Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte were astonished at this. They said to each other, “Truly, that lady has put some powerful spell on him.”
After a while Sir Pellias asked them to go away and leave him alone. They did, though they did not go willingly.

Sir Pellias lay there all day until the afternoon came. Then he roused himself and told his squire to bring him his armor. When Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte heard of this, they went to him and said, “Sir, what do you mean to do?” Sir Pellias answered, “I am going to try to reach the Lady Ettard.” They said, “What madness is this?” “I do not know,” said Sir Pellias, “but it seems to me that if I do not see the Lady Ettard and speak with her, I will surely die of longing for her.” They said, “Truly, this is madness.” He replied, “I do not know whether it is madness or whether I am caught in some enchantment.”

The squire brought Sir Pellias his armor as he had ordered and dressed him in it, so that he was armed from head to foot. Then Sir Pellias mounted his horse at once and rode out toward the castle of Grantmesnle.

When the Lady Ettard saw Sir Pellias riding up and down the meadow below the castle again, she called six of her best knights to her. She said to them, “Look, good sirs, there is the knight who brought so much shame on us yesterday. Now I order you to go out against him and punish him as he deserves.”
The six knights went and put on their armor. When they were ready, they rode out at once against Sir Pellias.

When Sir Pellias saw them coming, his heart filled with fury. He shouted in a mighty voice and charged at them. For a while they stood against him, but he could not be stopped. He fought with such terrible fury that they soon broke away from him and fled. He chased them around that field and knocked four of them from their horses. Then, when only two of the knights were left, Sir Pellias suddenly stopped fighting. He called out to those two knights, “Good sirs, I surrender to you.”

The two knights were greatly astonished. They were still full of fear at his strength, and they did not know why he would yield to them. Even so, they came and took hold of him and led him toward the castle. Sir Pellias said to himself, “Now they will bring me to the Lady Ettard, and I will be able to speak with her.” For this was the very reason he had let those two knights capture him.

But things did not go as Sir Pellias wished. When they had brought him close beneath the castle, the Lady Ettard called down to them from a window in the wall. She said, “What are you doing with that knight?” They answered, “We are bringing him to you, Lady.” She cried out fiercely, “Do not bring him to me! Take him, tie his hands behind his back, tie his feet beneath his horse’s belly, and send him back to his friends.”
Sir Pellias lifted his eyes to that window and cried out in great despair, “Lady, it was to you that I surrendered, and not to these unworthy knights.”
But the Lady Ettard cried out even more fiercely, “Drive him away, for I hate the sight of him.”
So the two knights did as the Lady Ettard said. They took Sir Pellias and tied him hand and foot on his horse. When they had done this, they let his horse carry him back to his friends in that way.

When Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte saw Sir Pellias come to them with his hands bound behind his back and his feet tied beneath his horse’s belly, they were filled with grief and despair. They untied the cords from his hands and feet and cried out to him, “Sir Knight, Sir Knight, are you not ashamed to allow such disgrace as this?” Sir Pellias shook and trembled as if he had a fever, and he cried out in despair, “I do not care what happens to me!” They said, “We do not mean yourself, Sir Knight. Think of the shame you bring on King Arthur and his Round Table!” Then Sir Pellias cried aloud, in a great and terrible voice, “I do not care about them, either.”

All this happened because of the powerful enchantment of the collar of emeralds, opal stones, and gold that Sir Pellias had given to the Lady Ettard and that she wore all the time. No man could withstand the enchantment of that collar. That is how Sir Pellias came to be bewitched and brought to such a depth of shame.
